newsitem.title: USA: Rocket fails to release NASA satellites.
newsitem.headline: Rocket fails to release NASA satellites.

text.p: A pair of NASA astronomy satellites failed to separate from a rocket after reaching orbit on Monday, dooming one and leaving scientists struggling to save the other, space agency officials said.
The two satellites were boosted into orbit by an air-launched Pegasus XL rocket but were not released from the rocket 11 minutes later as planned.

"Indications from the tracking stations show that (they are) still attached to the third stage," said J.R. Thompson of Orbital Sciences Corp., which manufactured the rocket for NASA. "It's quite disappointing for us to get this close and not finish the job the way we planned to do it."
The solid-fuelled Pegasus was launched from a L-1011 aircraft, which took off from NASA's Wallops Flight Facility at Wallops Island, Virginia.
The winged rocket was dropped from the aircraft and ignited its motor at 12:09 p.m. EST (1709 GMT) about 39,000 feet (11,900 meters) above the Atlantic, 100 miles (160 km) off the coast of Virginia.
The two satellites remained locked to the rocket 300 miles (480 km) high.

Scientists hope to get some data from the Satelite de Aplicaciones Cientificas (SAC-B), a joint project between NASA and Argentina's National Commission of Space Activities. Four of the satellite's five instruments may return useful data, said Jerre Hartman of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Centre.
"There is a chance that we can get some science out of SAC-B if we are lucky," he said.
SAC-B is supposed to study solar flares and gamma ray bursts, mysterious pulses of energy that intrigue astronomers.

The High Energy Transient Experiment (HETE) spacecraft, unable to deploy its electricty generating solar panels, was expected to become inoperable when its batteries ran out on Monday night, Hartman said.
HETE, a collaborative venture between the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and NASA, was supposed to probe the universe for gamma-ray and x-ray bursts.
Orbital Sciences Corp. and NASA's Goddard Space Flight Centre have formed investigation boards to determine what caused the mishap.
